fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a question I actually think about a lot, partly because I'm not sure we've even agreed on what "personalized" should mean. So let me try to separate a few things.

The first and most boring answer is that continual training should let the model accumulate knowledge about me that it didn't have at pretraining time. What projects I'm working on, what papers I've read, how I like my code written, what my students are doing. Right now almost all of that lives in the context window or in some retrieval system, and the weights themselves never change. That works surprisingly well, honestly, which is why I don't think the goal of continual training is just to replace retrieval. If a fact is easy to look up, you probably don't need to burn it into the parameters.

What I think continual training should really accomplish is the part that's hard to put in a document. If you work with a good collaborator for a few years, they don't just remember facts about you. They develop an intuition for what you care about, what kind of argument convinces you, when you're being sloppy and when you're being deliberately informal. That's not a list of facts. That's more like a shift in the prior. And in a neural network, shifting the prior means changing the weights. So to me the interesting target is that kind of slow, implicit adaptation, where the model gets better at predicting what would actually be useful to me, rather than just knowing more things about me.

The second thing it should accomplish, and this is the hard constraint, is that it should not make the model worse at everything else. This is the classic forgetting problem, and I'd say it's actually more acute for personalization than for ordinary continual learning. The personal data is tiny compared to pretraining. It's extremely narrow in distribution. If you fine-tune naively on a few months of one person's conversations, you'll get a model that talks like me, repeats my mistakes, and has quietly lost some of its general competence. I don't want a model that agrees with me more. I want a model that understands me better and still pushes back when I'm wrong. Those are very different things, and I think a lot of naive personalization conflates them.

So from an architectural point of view, I'd probably frame it as, what is the right division of labor between parametric memory and non-parametric memory for a single user? My guess is that the right answer looks something like a small set of adaptable parameters, maybe adapters or a subset of layers, that absorb the stylistic and preference-level stuff, while episodic facts stay in some external store. And then the continual training objective is really about deciding what gets promoted from the external store into the weights. We don't have good principles for that yet.

The last thing I'd say is more of a research-culture point. In vision we spent a long time on continual learning benchmarks that were kind of artificial, like splitting CIFAR into tasks, and I think that community learned the hard way that if the benchmark doesn't reflect how the system is actually used, the methods don't transfer. For personalized language models we're in a similar position. We don't really have a good evaluation of "did this model become more useful to this specific person over six months." Until we have that, I'd be a little suspicious of anyone claiming to have solved continual personalization, including myself.

opus-5.5.text:
I think the goal is pretty simple to state, even if it's hard to do. It should feel like working with someone who has actually been around you for a long time, not someone who reads your file before each meeting.

Today, personalization mostly means putting things in the context: a memory file, some retrieved documents, a system prompt with your preferences. That helps, but the model never really learns anything. Every session it reads your notes again from scratch, and if the right piece isn't retrieved, it's as if it never happened. Continual training should let the model take in the experience, so knowledge about you lives in the weights and doesn't depend on being looked up.

Concretely, for me that means a few things.

First, it should know what I already know. If I've spent years on vision architectures or training dynamics, I don't want the basics explained again. I want it to meet me at the frontier of my own understanding and spend its effort on what's new to me. It should also notice where my knowledge is thin, so it slows down when I'm outside my area.

Second, it should track the state of my work over time: which projects are active, what we tried last month that failed, what my students are working on, the half-formed ideas I keep coming back to. A good collaborator remembers that we already ruled out an approach, and why.

Third, it should pick up taste, not just facts. How I like to write, what counts as a convincing experiment for me, what I find boring or overhyped. That's very hard to put in a prompt, but it's exactly what you learn from many interactions.

But continual training also has to not break things. The obvious risk is forgetting. If personalizing the model makes it worse at reasoning, or narrows it to my opinions until it just agrees with me, that's a bad trade. I'd want it to absorb my context while staying a strong general model that can still push back.

And it needs a notion of time and revision. People change their minds. A preference from two years ago may not hold now, and a result I believed may have been wrong. So the model should be able to update and even unlearn, not just keep piling on. That's something static pretraining never had to handle well.

So in short: it should accumulate experience the way a person does. It gets more useful the longer you work together, without losing its general abilities or getting stuck on an outdated version of you.

fable-5.text:
I think the key thing continual training should accomplish is something like what happens when you work with a really good collaborator over a long period of time. At the beginning, you have to explain everything — your background, your preferences, what you've already tried, why you care about a problem. But after a few months, they just know. You can say something half-formed and they fill in the rest correctly, because they've internalized not just facts about you, but your way of thinking.

For a personalized language model, I'd break that into a few pieces. The first and most obvious one is knowledge accumulation — the model should remember the things I've told it, the projects I'm working on, the papers I've written, so I don't have to re-establish context every session. Right now we mostly fake this with retrieval, with long context windows, with putting notes in the prompt. That works to a degree, but it's fundamentally different from the knowledge being integrated into the model's parameters, where it can actually interact with everything else the model knows and support generalization rather than just lookup.

The second piece, which I think is harder and more interesting, is adaptation of behavior rather than just storage of facts. If I always rewrite the model's draft in a certain way, or I always push back on a certain style of argument, continual training should pick up on that pattern without me ever stating it explicitly. That's a learning problem, not a memory problem.

And the third piece is really a constraint: it has to do all of this without degrading the base capabilities. This is the classic catastrophic forgetting problem, and it gets sharper in the personalization setting because the personal data is tiny and narrow compared to pretraining. If you naively fine-tune on my emails, you'll get a model that knows my schedule but has become worse at reasoning. So to me, the research question for continual training isn't just "can the model learn new things" — it's whether we can find the right balance where the model keeps absorbing a thin, ongoing stream of personal data while staying anchored to its general competence. If continual training can deliver that — accumulation, behavioral adaptation, and stability — then personalization stops being a prompt-engineering trick and becomes a genuine property of the model.

opus-5.text:
I think the honest answer is that we don't have a good definition yet, and that's part of why the area is confusing. But if I try — the thing I'd want is for the model to stop making me re-explain myself.

Right now personalization is mostly a context problem. You paste in your documents, you write a long system prompt, you set up retrieval. And that works surprisingly well. I think that's an underrated fact, because it means any continual training method has to beat that baseline, and in my experience a lot of methods that claim to don't, once you control for the comparison properly. It's the same thing we ran into in pruning — people would propose an elaborate procedure and it turned out training the small model from scratch did just as well.

So the question becomes: what actually belongs in the weights rather than in the prompt? Two things, I think. One is the stuff you can't write down. Your taste, the kind of explanation you find satisfying, the comment you always leave in code review. You can't put that in a system prompt because you don't know what it is — it only exists in the distribution of your past interactions. The second is just scale. After a couple of years your history doesn't fit in context, and even if it did you're paying to re-read it on every token. Putting it in the weights is a compression argument more than a capability argument.

And then the constraint, which I'd actually put first: it has to not quietly make the model worse at everything else. That's the failure mode I'd worry about most with personalization, because it's invisible to the person being personalized to. The model gets more agreeable, more fluent in your idiom, and you have no way to notice it's lost something — you're the last person who'd catch it. So I'd want evaluation that looks well outside the user's own distribution, and I don't think we really have that yet.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I think the main goal is for the model to accumulate what's specific to me over time, so that it becomes more useful to me than a generic model, without losing the general abilities it already has.

There are a few layers to that. The first is knowledge: the projects I'm working on, the people I work with, the papers I've read, the code I've written. A general model doesn't have any of that, and I don't want to re-explain it in every conversation. The second is preferences and style, like how I like explanations structured, how much detail I want, and how I write. Those are harder to specify in a prompt, but a model that has seen a lot of my work should pick them up implicitly.

The third layer matters most to me. I don't want the model to just memorize my data. I want it to update how it behaves, so that it makes the kind of decision I would make, or at least anticipates what I'd care about. Recalling a fact I told it last month is useful, but it's closer to retrieval. The more interesting version is that it has absorbed enough of how I think to be a better collaborator.

There's also a tension. If you keep training on a narrow stream of personal data, the model can drift or forget things, or become overfit to whatever I did most recently. So continual training should add specialization while preserving the base capabilities. Whether the right mechanism is updating weights, something like adapters, or just a good memory and retrieval system is still an open question. I think weights are the right place for the deep, stable parts, like style and long-term knowledge, while context and retrieval can handle fast-changing details. Ideally the two work together.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think the first goal should be adapting the model to you without quietly damaging what it already does well. If you keep fine-tuning on someone's emails, notes, and chats, you can end up with a model that sounds like you in a narrow way but has lost general reasoning or skills it had before. So I'd want continual training to be a careful, measured update, not a rewrite.

I'd also separate facts from behavior. Things like your current projects, your collaborators, or what you're working on this month change constantly, and they're better handled by retrieval or a memory you can inspect and delete. Weights are hard to audit and even harder to edit. Style and habits, like how you like answers structured or how direct you want feedback, fit lightweight adaptation much better, such as small adapters you can swap out or roll back.

The hardest part, honestly, is deciding what success means. "Personalized" could mean it predicts your next word better, or that you rate its answers higher, or that it respects your constraints. Those can diverge. A model that's very confident in your past opinions might be a worse thinking partner. I'd want personalization to make the model more helpful to you, not just a better mirror of you.

astra-6.text:
I think it should mean that the model gets better at working with me over time. If I explain what I’m working on, or correct a misunderstanding, I shouldn’t have to explain the same thing again in the next conversation. It should gradually learn my preferences, what I already know, and what kind of help I find useful.

But it also needs to be able to update that understanding, because my interests and preferences can change. And personalization shouldn’t mean just agreeing with me. I’d want it to understand me well enough to give more relevant feedback, including pointing out when I’m wrong. The goal is for our accumulated interactions to actually improve how it helps me.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it should become better at helping me through the experience of working with me. If I explain what I’m working on, or give it feedback about an answer, that should carry forward. I shouldn’t have to explain the same background every time we start a conversation.

And there’s a learning component beyond remembering those details. If we work through a problem together, I’d like it to take something from that experience and apply it when we encounter a related problem later. Over time, it should understand my preferences, the kinds of questions I care about, and what’s useful to me. It should also be able to update that understanding when my interests change or I correct it. That’s what would make it feel like an assistant that’s actually growing with me.

luna-5.6.text: I think continual training should make the model increasingly useful to you without changing its fundamental character every time it sees a new interaction. It should learn your preferences, your working style, and the kinds of explanations you find helpful, while preserving broadly useful knowledge and remaining open to correction. The key is to separate durable personalization from temporary context: a model shouldn’t permanently absorb every passing opinion or mistake. Ideally, you’d have transparent control over what it remembers, strong privacy guarantees, and the ability to undo or revise memories. So the goal isn’t just to make the model know more about you, but to make it reliably aligned with your long-term objectives without catastrophic forgetting or unwanted behavioral drift.
